samples.question: Which patients have severe coronary artery disease (outcome 3 or 4) with marked ST depression?
samples.reference_answer: Patients with severe to critical CAD include: Patient P1006 (62-year-old female, diagnosis outcome 3, oldpeak 3.6 downsloping, cholesterol 268.0 mg/dL), Patient P1023 (58-year-old male, diagnosis outcome 3, oldpeak 3.2, cholesterol 224.0 mg/dL), and Patient P1024 (60-year-old male, diagnosis outcome 4 - very severe CAD, oldpeak 2.4 flat slope, exercise-induced angina True, and LV hypertrophy).
retrieved_contexts: Mechanisms and Clinical Significance of ST-Segment Depression: ST-segment depression (measured as the 'oldpeak' value in millimeters on ECG during exercise stress testing) is an electrocardiographic indicator of subendocardial myocardial ischemia. During cardiac stress or exercise, myocardial oxygen demand increases. When stenosed coronary arteries cannot supply adequate blood flow, the subendocardium becomes ischemic, altering the electrical potential during ventricular repolarization. Significant ST depression is defined as horizontal or downsloping displacement >= 1.0 mm (0.1 mV) occurring 60 to 80 ms after the J-point. Downsloping ST depression indicates severe multi-vessel CAD and high cardiovascular risk, whereas flat ST depression indicates moderate ischemia, and upsloping ST depression may represent milder ischemia or rapid tachycardia.

Symptoms of Heart Disease and Coronary Artery Disease: Common symptoms of coronary artery disease (CAD) and heart disease include chest pain or discomfort (angina pectoris), pressure, tightness, or squeezing sensations in the chest or arms that may radiate to the neck, jaw, shoulder, or back. Additional symptoms include shortness of breath (dyspnea) during exertion or rest, unexplained fatigue, lightheadedness, dizziness, palpitations, cold sweats, and swelling in the legs, ankles, or feet (edema). In some patients, especially women and elderly individuals, symptoms may be atypical, presenting as nausea, indigestion, epigastric discomfort, or silent ischemia without classic chest pain.

samples.question: Identify patients with hypercholesterolemia with serum cholesterol level exceeding 280 mg/dL and exercise-induced angina.
samples.reference_answer: Patients meeting both criteria are Patient P1001 (cholesterol 286.0 mg/dL, exercise induced angina True, diagnosis outcome 2) and Patient P1007 (cholesterol 354.0 mg/dL, exercise induced angina True, diagnosis outcome 0).
retrieved_contexts: Causes and Pathophysiology of High Cholesterol (Hypercholesterolemia): High serum cholesterol (hypercholesterolemia, typically defined as total cholesterol > 200 mg/dL or LDL > 130 mg/dL, with severe hypercholesterolemia exceeding 240-280 mg/dL) is caused by a combination of genetic factors (such as familial hypercholesterolemia and LDL receptor mutations) and lifestyle factors. Major lifestyle causes include diets rich in saturated and trans fats, physical inactivity, obesity, and smoking. Secondary medical causes include type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, chronic kidney disease, and cholestatic liver disease. Elevated low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles infiltrate arterial endothelial walls, undergoing oxidative modification and promoting foam cell formation, atheromatous plaque development, and coronary artery narrowing.

Exercise-Induced Angina and Myocardial Ischemia Pathophysiology: Exercise-induced angina (exang) occurs when physical exertion increases heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and left ventricular contractility, sharply escalating myocardial oxygen consumption. In patients with fixed atherosclerotic coronary stenoses, coronary vascular reserve is exhausted, preventing compensatory vasodilation. The resulting supply-demand mismatch causes acute transient subendocardial ischemia, lactic acidosis, and activation of cardiac nociceptive fibers perceived as angina pectoris. The presence of exercise-induced angina strongly correlates with obstructive coronary artery disease.

Symptoms of Heart Disease and Coronary Artery Disease: Common symptoms of coronary artery disease (CAD) and heart disease include chest pain or discomfort (angina pectoris), pressure, tightness, or squeezing sensations in the chest or arms that may radiate to the neck, jaw, shoulder, or back. Additional symptoms include shortness of breath (dyspnea) during exertion or rest, unexplained fatigue, lightheadedness, dizziness, palpitations, cold sweats, and swelling in the legs, ankles, or feet (edema). In some patients, especially women and elderly individuals, symptoms may be atypical, presenting as nausea, indigestion, epigastric discomfort, or silent ischemia without classic chest pain.

Cardiovascular Disease Risk Factors and Prevention: Major non-modifiable risk factors for cardiovascular disease include advancing age (especially men > 45 and women > 55), male biological sex, and family history of premature coronary heart disease. Modifiable risk factors include systemic hypertension (resting blood pressure > 130/80 mmHg), hyperlipidemia (elevated total cholesterol and LDL, low HDL), cigarette smoking, insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus (fasting blood sugar > 120 mg/dL), obesity (elevated BMI), sedentary lifestyle, chronic psychological stress, and unhealthy diet. Managing blood pressure, lowering LDL cholesterol, controlling blood glucose, exercising regularly, and smoking cessation substantially reduce cardiovascular morbidity.

Impact of Elevated Fasting Blood Sugar and Diabetes on Coronary Vasculature: Fasting blood sugar (fbs) exceeding 120 mg/dL indicates impaired fasting glucose or overt diabetes mellitus. Chronic hyperglycemia accelerates non-enzymatic glycation of arterial proteins, stimulates reactive oxygen species (ROS), induces endothelial nitric oxide synthase dysfunction, and promotes systemic low-grade vascular inflammation. Diabetic patients with coronary artery disease frequently suffer from diffuse multi-vessel involvement, higher incidence of silent myocardial infarction due to autonomic neuropathy, and poorer post-revascularization outcomes.
